title: Why reasoning models will generalize / An unexpected RL Renaissance (on RLVR)
pub: Interconnects (Substack); author at the Allen Institute for AI (Ai2), lead on Tülu 3
author: Nathan Lambert

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Lambert supports the proposition’s jagged-capability component: he expects rapid and broad improvement but explicitly rejects universal superiority, emphasizing domain-specific performance and cost trade-offs. His source does not materially address legal workflow redesign, user expertise or human verification, so its support is narrower than the full cluster synthesis.
qs: The nature of this coming *generalization* is not that these models are one size fits all, best in all cases: speed, intelligence, price, etc.
Especially, where the standard models match the reasoning models abilities, you’ll be paying way more for the same performance.

kp.k: Reasoning generalization rests on architectural fit
kp.d: Lambert argues that chain-of-thought reasoning suits language models because it breaks information processing into smaller steps and stores intermediate information in the context window. He explicitly identifies this fit as the assumption underpinning his prediction that reasoning training will generalize beyond code and mathematics, with ample evidence expected by the end of 2025. His focus is text domains; translation to other modalities is less clear to him. These are cross-domain AI claims, not findings about legal services.
qs: Chain of thought reasoning allows information to be naturally processed in smaller chunks, allowing the large, brute force probability distribution to work one token at a time.
Chain of thought, while allowing more compute per important token, also allows the models to *store* intermediate information in their context window without needing explicit recurrence.
By the end of 2025 we should have ample evidence of this given the pace of the technological development.
By domains I’m focused on text domains. I expect improvements across all modalities, but how it is translated is less clear to me.

kp.k: Compute allocation offers another generalization mechanism
kp.d: Lambert presents reasoning training as teaching models to allocate more computation to harder problems, a capability he considers fundamental across tasks. He qualifies this mechanism by acknowledging that contemporary reasoning models do not yet allocate computation perfectly.
qs: a far more practical way to view the new style of training is a method that teaches the model to be better at allocating more compute to harder problems.
If the skill is compute allocation, it is fundamental to the models handling a variety of tasks.
Today’s reasoning models do not solve this perfectly, but they open the door for doing so precisely.

kp.k: Predicted gains remain uneven and computationally costly
kp.d: For the next 0–3 years from January 2025, Lambert forecasts superhuman performance in verifiable domains such as code and mathematics, higher peak performance in unexpected and not necessarily verifiable domains, and improvements on long-tail tasks at higher inference costs. He rejects a universally optimal model across speed, intelligence and price, and warns that reasoning models can cost more without improving performance where ordinary models already match them.
qs: A *realistic* outcome for reasoning heavy models in the next 0-3 years is a world where:
Reasoning trained models are superhuman on tasks with verifiable domains, like those with initial progress: Code, math, etc.
Reasoning trained models are still *better* in performance at the long-tail of tasks, but *worse* in cost given the high inference costs of long-context.
Especially, where the standard models match the reasoning models abilities, you’ll be paying way more for the same performance.

kp.k: Safety research supplies early evidence beyond mathematics
kp.d: Lambert cites OpenAI’s Deliberative Alignment and Trading Inference-Time Compute for Adversarial Robustness as evidence that reasoning methods transfer to safety policies and jailbreaking. He contrasts context-sensitive, subjective safety decisions with mathematics and coding. The claim of strong out-of-distribution safety generalization is quoted from OpenAI’s deliberative alignment release, rather than presented as Lambert’s independent experimental finding.
qs: These papers show their new methods can be translated to various safety domains, i.e. model safety policies and jailbreaking.
The deliberative alignment paper shows them integrating a softer reward signal into the reasoning training — having a language model check how the safety policies apply to outputs.
we find that deliberative alignment enables strong generalization to out-of-distribution safety scenarios.

kp.k: Generative reward judges could expand reasoning training
kp.d: Lambert predicts that model-generated reward judgments will extend reasoning training into many domains, while noting that these judgments are not ground truth and could be vulnerable to reward hacking. He argues that progress requires both better output generators and better reward judges, potentially forming an iterative improvement process. His suggestion that o1 and related models were trained mostly with explicit code verifiers is qualified as likely; these verifiers are training mechanisms, not human checking of professional work.
qs: This generative verifier for safety is not a ground truth signal and *could* theoretically be subject to reward hacking, but it was avoided.
Generative verifiers will be crucial to expanding this training to countless domains — they’re easy to use and largely a new development.
All of the progress here relies on continued progress on both generators and verifiers.
o1 et al. were likely trained with mostly explicit, code verifiers.

kp.k: Benchmarks and user anecdotes suggest broader usefulness
kp.d: As early indications of generalization, Lambert reports strong DeepSeek-R1 results on a creative-writing and humor leaderboard and Humanity’s Last Exam, including accuracy and calibration error. He tentatively suggests reasoning training may help uncertainty calibration. He also cites ChatBotArena standings and friends’ favorable experiences with o1-pro, which are reported evaluations and anecdotes rather than controlled evidence that reasoning training alone caused the gains.
qs: Examples include a [creative writing and humor leaderboard](https://eqbench.com/creative_writing.html) or the brand-new, extremely challenging benchmark from the Center for AI Safety and Scale AI — [Humanity’s Last Exam](https://agi.safe.ai/).
Oh, and yes, it’s best on both accuracy and the new metric “calibration error” which is designed to have the model express its own uncertainty.
Calibration is a long-sought behavior in traditional LMs and turns out maybe reasoning training helps it?
A lot of my friends find o1-pro to be clearly the most useful AI model in their daily workflows

kp.k: Amodei describes reasoning as a continuous spectrum
kp.d: In a quoted interview, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei frames reasoning as an emergent consequence of larger-scale, outcome-based reinforcement learning, rather than a wholly separate method. He anticipates fluid combinations of reasoning and other tasks. Separately, Lambert speculates that the newest Claude 3.5 Sonnet models already received some training on verifiable outcomes and predicts that reasoning benefits will be incorporated into ordinary AI products.
qs: We see it more as a continuous spectrum — the ability for models to think, reflect on their own thinking, and ultimately produce a result.
It’s more like an emergent property, a consequence of training the model in an outcome-based way at a larger scale.
I think that will lead to something that continuously interpolates between reasoning and other tasks, fluidly combining reasoning with everything else models do.
The newest Claude 3.5 Sonnet models are very likely already trained to some extent* with RL on verifiable outcomes.

kp.k: DeepSeek authors report emergent reflection and alternative exploration
kp.d: Lambert quotes the DeepSeek-R1 paper’s authors as reporting that reflection and exploration of alternative approaches emerge through interaction with the reinforcement-learning environment rather than explicit programming. The quoted account attributes improved DeepSeek-R1-Zero capabilities to these behaviors as test-time computation increases; this is the paper authors’ interpretation carried by Lambert.
qs: Behaviors such as reflection—where the model revisits and reevaluates its previous steps—and the exploration of alternative approaches to problem-solving arise spontaneously.
These behaviors are not explicitly programmed but instead emerge as a result of the model’s interaction with the reinforcement learning environment.
This spontaneous development significantly enhances DeepSeek-R1-Zero’s reasoning capabilities, enabling it to tackle more challenging tasks with greater efficiency and accuracy.

kp.k: Mature infrastructure distinguishes this reinforcement-learning wave
kp.d: In February 2025, Lambert contrasts the current reasoning-model wave with the Alpaca, Vicuña and Dolly era, when basic instruction tuning predominated and tooling and dataset limitations hindered substantive RLHF replications. He reports that stable open-source tools, including TRL, OpenRLHF, veRL and Open Instruct, are already being used successfully, while companies have funding in place. He predicts that the new wave will have deeper results and impact than the earlier Alpaca moment.
qs: When models such as Alpaca, Vicuña, Dolly, etc. were coming out they were all built on basic instruction tuning.
Even though RLHF was the motivation of these experiments, tooling, and lack of datasets made complete and substantive replications rare.
With reasoning models, everyone already has raised money for their AI companies, open-source tooling for RLHF exists and is stable, and everyone is already feeling the AGI.
While this will feel like the Alpaca moment from 2 years ago, it will produce much deeper results and impact.

kp.k: Reinforcement learning could become the central training paradigm
kp.d: Lambert argues that reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards works on older models and offers substantial opportunities for improvement. He distinguishes RLHF’s necessary but insufficient role in ChatGPT from the prospective role of reasoning-oriented RL as the primary driver of future language-model development. The possibility that post-training becomes simply training is explicitly a forecast, not an established transition.
qs: Given it is becoming obvious that RL with verifiable rewards works on old models — why did the AI community sleep on the potential of these reasoning models?
RLHF was necessary, but not sufficient for ChatGPT.
RL training like for reasoning could become the primary driving force of future LM developments.
There’s a path for “post-training” to just be called “training” in the future.

kp.k: Inference-time compute is distinct from new RL methods
kp.d: Lambert cautions against equating the new reinforcement-learning developments with self-play or inference-time computation, describing those concepts as inspirations or side effects rather than the core advance. He separately argues that greater inference expenditure can improve the likelihood of a correct answer with any model, so that mechanism is not unique to the new RL approach.
qs: Self-play, inference-time compute, and other popular terms related to this movement are more “side quests” than core to the RL developments.
They’re both either inspirations or side-effects of good RL.
Inference time compute is also orthogonal.
With any model, spending more on inference makes it more likely that you will arrive at the correct answer.
This is foundational to modern AI stacks, but not necessarily the same thing as pursuing the new RL ideas.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Lambert predicts that reasoning training will improve language models beyond code and mathematics, with uneven performance gains and higher inference costs.
pts.d: These are cross-domain claims about AI development, not claims about legal services. In the January article, Lambert argues that chain-of-thought reasoning fits language models' information processing and can teach better allocation of computation to difficult problems. He predicts superhuman performance in verifiable domains, higher peak performance in unexpected and not necessarily verifiable domains, and improved long-tail performance at greater cost. He expects reasoning-training benefits to spread throughout AI products rather than remain confined to a separate model category. In February, he predicts that reasoning-style reinforcement learning could become the principal driver of language-model development and that the emerging wave of open reasoning models will have deeper effects than the earlier Alpaca-era instruction-tuning wave.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Lambert supports his predictions with a mechanistic argument, cited safety research, benchmark observations, user anecdotes, and evidence of existing RL infrastructure.
pts.d: Lambert's central argument is that chain of thought provides intermediate storage and additional computation suited to language-model architectures. He cites OpenAI's Deliberative Alignment and Trading Inference-Time Compute for Adversarial Robustness as examples of reasoning methods extending to safety policies and jailbreak resistance; these are attributed research results rather than his own experiments. He reports strong DeepSeek-R1 results on creative-writing and humor evaluations and Humanity's Last Exam, including accuracy and calibration, and strong reasoning-model positions in ChatBotArena. He offers friends' reports of o1-pro usefulness as anecdotal evidence, distinct from benchmarking. The February article points to frequent new models, training results and datasets, and stable RL tooling as the basis for expecting faster and deeper replication than in the RLHF era. The supplied text does not provide numerical benchmark tables or controlled estimates of the predicted general gains. His suggestion that Claude 3.5 Sonnet already uses RL on verifiable outcomes is explicitly an inference, informed partly by observed behavior and Dario Amodei's quoted comments, not a confirmed training disclosure.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The January article anticipates evidence of generalization by the end of 2025 and outlines a zero-to-three-year outlook, explicitly qualified by domain differences, costs and verifier progress.
pts.d: The January 28, 2025 article predicts ample evidence by year-end and describes a realistic outlook over the following zero to three years. Lambert principally means text domains; he expects multimodal gains but is less clear about their mechanism. His forecast assumes chain of thought is a natural fit for language-model reasoning. It does not imply universal superiority across speed, price and intelligence: standard models may match reasoning models at lower cost. Expansion through generative verifiers depends on progress in both generators and verifiers. Here, a verifier means an automated training reward or judging mechanism, not human checking of professional work. Lambert acknowledges that generative safety verification is not ground truth and may theoretically invite reward hacking. The February 13 article predicts a future shift toward RL-centered training without a fixed deadline and distinguishes increased inference spending from the new RL methods themselves.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are model developers, open-source researchers, AI product providers and users, including nontechnical users; the source identifies no legal-market segment.
pts.d: Developers and researchers gain opportunities to improve existing models using established RL tooling and to broaden training through generative verifiers. AI companies may integrate reasoning into ordinary products rather than offer it solely as a distinct mode. Users may obtain better answers across more tasks, while paying more where additional computation is necessary or where reasoning adds no advantage over standard models. Lambert reports that nontechnical users already benefit from seeing the reasoning process, alongside anecdotal workflow benefits for his friends. Neither article makes a specific prediction about lawyers, law firms, clients, legal employment or access to justice.
